newsitem.title: USA: Cancer institute promises clearer mammogram advice.
newsitem.headline: Cancer institute promises clearer mammogram advice.

text.p: The top U.S. cancer official on Wednesday promised women in their 40s that they would have clearer information on whether they should have mammograms.

National Cancer Institute director Dr. Richard Klausner acknowledged to a Senate panel that an NCI advisory panel's recent refusal to state whether women in that age group should have the breast cancer screening had muddied the waters. That panel basically said women should make up their own minds.

A separate advisory panel charged with drawing up a more definitive report will meet in three weeks and Klausner said the goal, at a minimum, would be to lay out clearly the benefits and drawbacks for screening.

He did not predict whether the panel would opt for formal clinical guidelines or restate the pros and cons in a way that is more useful for women and their doctors, but he said he thought the earlier panel understated the benefits and overstated the risks.

Health experts agree that mammograms save the lives of women age 50-69 but do not advise them routinely for women in their 20s and 30s. But the data on the "transitional decade" of the 40s has been less clear.

The NCI in 1993 stopped recommending the X-rays for 40 to 49-year-olds but recently decided new research warranted another look at the policy. Summarizing the new data to a Senate Appropriations subcommittee on Wednesday, Klausner said screening for women in their 40s would reduce mortality by about 15 percent -- or 1,600 lives a year.

Although the lifetime risk of breast cancer is one in eight, the risk for women in their 40s is about 1 in 66. The risk of death from cancer that develops while a woman is in her 40s is 1 in 190. Screening for these women would reduce the risk of death to about 1 in 220, he said.

Breast cancer is emotional partly because it is probably the disease women dread most and because the cancer rates have soared in the past few decades. But researchers have also shown that women overestimate their risk of breast cancer.

Although breast cancer is the leading cause of death for women in their 40s, about three-fourths of the cases occur in older women. Breast cancer is not the leading cause of death, or even the leading cause of cancer death, for older women -- heart disease kills far more.

The recent outcry over mammogram guidelines has provoked unusual moves by the Senate, which does not routinely get involved in the nuts and bolts of health guidelines. But the NCI recommendations could impact health insurance policies and could also play a role in Medicare or Medicaid policy.

The Senate on Tuesday passed a nonbinding resolution calling for the NCI to reconsider its stance on mammograms. On Wednesday, the subcommittee led by Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, grilled Klausner and other health officials on the mammogram policy.
